title: Jeremiah 12:1–13
context: Jeremiah 12:1–13 has two voices. In 12:1–4 Jeremiah brings a complaint to the LORD: “You are righteous, LORD, when I contend with you; yet I would like to plead a case with you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper?” He grants God’s righteousness, asks why the treacherous flourish, appeals to the LORD who tests his heart (12:3; compare 11:20), and laments a land that mourns because its people say, “He won’t see our latter end.” (12:4). The question stands alongside Habakkuk 1:2–4 and 1:13, Psalm 73:3–17, and Job 21:7, which are named here without being harmonized. The complaint follows the plot against Jeremiah in his hometown of Anathoth (11:18–23), and 12:6 warns that his own brothers and father’s house have dealt treacherously with him. In 12:5–13 the LORD answers, though not by explaining the prosperity of the wicked. He first warns Jeremiah that harder trials lie ahead (12:5–6), then laments that he has forsaken his house and given “the dearly beloved of my soul” into the hand of her enemies (12:7–13). The LORD’s answer runs from 12:5 through 12:13; within it the LORD sometimes speaks of himself in the third person (12:12–13), and some readers hear the prophet’s voice blending with the LORD’s in these lines. The shepherds who destroy the vineyard (12:10) are taken by some as foreign rulers and by others as Judah’s own leaders. Both traditions treat Jeremiah’s honest complaint, and the confession that God is righteous even when his ways are hidden, as largely shared ground; questions about how God uses hostile agents are treated in the existing box at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: You are righteous, LORD, when I contend with you; yet I would like to plead a case with you. Why does the way of the wicked prosper? Why are they all at ease who deal very treacherously?
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says, “You are righteous, LORD, when I contend with you”, and still asks why the way of the wicked prospers. Arminian readers note that the prophet holds faith and complaint together, and they compare Habakkuk 1:13, Psalm 73:3, and Job 21:7, named here without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah begins by confessing God’s righteousness before he states his case, so the complaint is made within trust rather than against it. They read the question of the prospering wicked as largely shared ground, an honest lament both traditions encourage God’s people to bring before him.

verses.text: You have planted them. Yes, they have taken root. They grow. Yes, they produce fruit. You are near in their mouth, and far from their heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says of the wicked, “You have planted them. Yes, they have taken root.” Arminian readers note that the prophet traces even the prosperity of the wicked to God’s hand, and they see the sharp line “You are near in their mouth, and far from their heart” as a portrait of empty religious speech.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same confession that the wicked flourish only as God allows them to be planted, which they read within God’s providence over all things. They see the line about lips and heart as a searching word about worship that is outwardly correct but inwardly far from God.

verses.text: But you, LORD, know me. You see me, and test my heart toward you. Pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah says, “But you, LORD, know me. You see me, and test my heart toward you.” Arminian readers note the echo of 11:20, where the LORD is the one “who tests the heart and the mind”, and they see the prophet resting his case on God’s knowledge of his integrity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same echo and read the prayer for the wicked to be pulled out like sheep for slaughter as a plea for God’s justice, not personal revenge, which also echoes Jeremiah’s own words in 11:19. They see in it a cry both traditions recognize from the lament psalms.

verses.text: How long will the land mourn, and the herbs of the whole country wither? Because of the wickedness of those who dwell therein, the animals and birds are consumed; because they said, “He won’t see our latter end.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jeremiah asks how long the land will mourn because of the wickedness of its people, who say, “He won’t see our latter end.” Arminian readers note that the land itself suffers from human sin, and they see the people’s words as presumption that God will not hold them to account.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link between human sin and the suffering of the land and its creatures. They observe the contrast with Psalm 73:17, where the psalmist “considered their latter end”, named here without harmonizing, and they read the people’s denial as a refusal to fear God’s judgment.

verses.text: “If you have run with the footmen, and they have wearied you, then how can you contend with horses? Though in a land of peace you are secure, yet how will you do in the pride of the Jordan?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers, “If you have run with the footmen, and they have wearied you, then how can you contend with horses?” Arminian readers note that God does not explain the prosperity of the wicked but prepares Jeremiah for greater trials, calling him to persevere in his calling.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same surprising answer, which strengthens the prophet rather than satisfying his question. They read the pride of the Jordan as the dense thickets along the river, a place of danger, though the exact sense is discussed, and they see God’s answer as a call to endurance.

verses.text: For even your brothers, and the house of your father, even they have dealt treacherously with you! Even they have cried aloud after you! Don’t believe them, though they speak beautiful words to you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD warns that even Jeremiah’s brothers and his father’s house have dealt treacherously with him: “Don’t believe them, though they speak beautiful words to you.” Arminian readers note the link with the plot from Anathoth (11:21), and they see the painful truth that opposition can come from those closest to us.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same link with 11:18–23 and read the warning as God’s protective care for his servant. They observe that the prophet’s loneliness becomes part of his calling, and they see in the verse a sober reminder that pleasant words do not always reveal a person’s heart.

verses.text: “I have forsaken my house. I have cast off my heritage. I have given the dearly beloved of my soul into the hand of her enemies.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I have forsaken my house. I have cast off my heritage.” Arminian readers note the grief in the LORD’s words, who gives “the dearly beloved of my soul” into the hand of her enemies, and they see a God who judges his people with real sorrow over their unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same grief and read the forsaking as covenant judgment on a people who have turned away, not the end of God’s purposes for them. They observe that the LORD still calls Judah his heritage and beloved even as he hands her over, a tension both traditions hold.

verses.text: My heritage has become to me as a lion in the forest. She has uttered her voice against me. Therefore I have hated her.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says his heritage has become like a lion in the forest that roars against him, “Therefore I have hated her.” Arminian readers note that the language of hatred describes rejection in judgment, rather than a fixed hostility, and they see it as the response to a people who have turned against God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the word hated in its covenant setting, as God’s withdrawal of favor in judgment, and they caution against pressing it beyond its context. They observe that the image of a roaring lion reverses the picture of a beloved heritage, showing how deeply Judah has rebelled.

verses.text: Is my heritage to me as a speckled bird of prey? Are the birds of prey against her all around? Go, assemble all the animals of the field. Bring them to devour.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Is my heritage to me as a speckled bird of prey?” Arminian readers note that the image is uncertain, perhaps a bird of unusual markings attacked by other birds, and they see Judah pictured as surrounded by enemies who are invited to devour her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the exact sense of the speckled bird loosely, since translations differ. They read the summons of the animals of the field to devour as an announcement that God will allow hostile nations to come against his people.

verses.text: Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard. They have trodden my portion under foot. They have made my pleasant portion a desolate wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Many shepherds have destroyed my vineyard.” Arminian readers note that shepherds commonly stand for rulers, and they hold open whether foreign kings invading Judah or Judah’s own leaders are meant, seeing in either case a vineyard ruined by those who should have tended it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note both readings of the shepherds, and they compare the vineyard imagery found elsewhere in the prophets. They read the verse as God’s lament over his pleasant portion made a desolate wilderness, and they see responsibility placed on those who led or trampled it.

verses.text: They have made it a desolation. It mourns to me, being desolate. The whole land is made desolate, because no one cares.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the land has been made a desolation and mourns to him, “because no one cares.” Arminian readers note the poignant picture of a land grieving before God while its people remain indifferent, and they see the lack of care as the real tragedy behind the devastation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase no one cares may also be read as no one takes it to heart, and they see in it the spiritual indifference that the prophets often condemn. Both traditions treat the verse as a call to take God’s word and his judgments seriously.

verses.text: Destroyers have come on all the bare heights in the wilderness; for the sword of the LORD devours from the one end of the land even to the other end of the land. No flesh has peace.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that destroyers have come on all the bare heights, “for the sword of the LORD devours from the one end of the land even to the other end of the land.” Arminian readers note that the invading armies are described as the LORD’s sword, and they read this as God using nations in judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse attributes the destruction directly to the LORD’s sword, which they read within God’s sovereign rule over the nations.

verses.text: They have sown wheat, and have reaped thorns. They have exhausted themselves, and profit nothing. You will be ashamed of your fruits, because of the LORD’s fierce anger.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “They have sown wheat, and have reaped thorns.” Arminian readers note the image of futile labor and see it as the outcome of turning from God, with the people ashamed of their fruits because of the LORD’s fierce anger, a consequence of their own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reversal of sowing and reaping recalls the covenant curses, and they read the people’s shame as the fruit of their rebellion under God’s just anger. They observe that the LORD speaks of himself in the third person here, and some readers hear the prophet’s voice joining his.
